Tunica intima.description: The innermost coat, the part of the vein that touches the blood. It is a single layer of flat endothelial cells on a thin sheet of connective tissue, with few elastic fibres. The paired semilunar valve cusps are folds of this lining, reinforced with connective tissue, that stop blood flowing backwards, away from the heart.
clinical: When the valve cusps fail to close fully, blood leaks backwards, away from the heart, and pressure builds up in the vein. Failing valves in the leg veins are a major cause of varicose veins.
Injury to the endothelium, slow blood flow and a tendency to clot make up Virchow's triad, the basis of deep vein thrombosis. It usually forms in a deep vein of the leg.
The thin media lets a vein stretch easily when pressure rises. Chronic pressure in the leg veins can dilate and weaken the wall, which contributes to varicose veins.

Tunica adventitia.description: The outer coat and the thickest layer of a vein. It is made of collagen and elastic fibres with fibroblasts, longitudinal smooth muscle bundles, nerves and small vessels (vasa vasorum) that supply the wall. Perivascular fat lies just outside it.

clinical: Red blood cells carry oxygen on haemoglobin. In anaemia there are too few red cells or too little haemoglobin, so the tissues receive less oxygen.

parts.description: The endothelium is the single layer of flat endothelial cells that lines the lumen and is in direct contact with the blood. Its cells rest on a thin basement membrane (basal lamina), and their flattened nuclei bulge slightly into the lumen, so in a section it appears as a delicate, dark line along the inner edge of the wall. It forms a smooth, anticlotting surface, controls which substances pass into the wall, and releases nitric oxide and other mediators that keep the vessel relaxed.

The subendothelial layer is the thin zone of loose connective tissue that lies between the endothelium and the tunica media. It contains fine collagen fibrils, scattered elastic fibres and a few fibroblasts, and in large veins it may also hold some longitudinal smooth muscle cells. In a section it appears as a pale, sparsely cellular band just beneath the dark endothelial line, giving the lining its support.

The venous valve connective tissue cores are the fibrous central supports of the valve cusps. Each core is a band of collagen with some elastic fibres and fibroblasts that runs into the fold of intima, and it is covered on both faces by endothelium. This firm core gives the cusp enough strength to stay closed when blood pushes back against it, and in a section it shows as a pink fibrous strand inside a small inward fold of the lining.

Venous valve cusps are the paired, semilunar folds of tunica intima that project into the lumen of many veins of the limbs, especially the legs. Each cusp is a thin, endothelium-covered flap whose free edge points towards the heart, so blood flowing upwards pushes it flat against the wall and the vein stays open. When blood tries to flow back, the two cusps meet in the middle and close the lumen, which stops reflux; incompetent valves are a key cause of varicose veins.

The tunica media is the middle coat of the vein wall, lying between the intima and the adventitia. In veins it is thin, with only a few layers of circular smooth muscle cells set in collagen, far thinner than the media of an artery of the same size. This thin, easily distended wall lets veins act as capacitance vessels, holding about two thirds of the blood volume. In a section it is a narrow band of smooth muscle with elongated nuclei.

The tunica adventitia is the outermost coat of the vein wall, and in veins it is usually the thickest layer. It is made of loose connective tissue, mainly collagen and elastic fibres with fibroblasts, and it contains the vasa vasorum, the nervi vasorum and bundles of longitudinal smooth muscle. It merges gradually with the surrounding connective tissue, which anchors the vein in place; in a section it is the thick, pinkish, fibrous outer zone.

Longitudinal smooth muscle bundles are groups of smooth muscle cells running lengthwise along the vein inside the tunica adventitia, the outer coat. They are best developed in large veins, such as the inferior vena cava, and help set the tone of the vein wall. In a longitudinal section they show as bands of spindle-shaped cells with elongated nuclei, and in cross-section as small round profiles among the collagen of the adventitia.

Adventitial collagen bundles are the wavy bundles of type I collagen that form the main fibrous part of the tunica adventitia, the outer coat of the vein. They run mostly along the vessel in a shallow spiral, with elastic fibres between them, and they are slack when the vein is at rest. As pressure rises and the wall stretches, the bundles straighten and tighten, which limits how far the vein can distend; in a section they appear as pink, wavy fibres filling the outer wall.

Vasa vasorum ('vessels of the vessels') are the small arteries, veins and capillaries that supply the wall of a larger vessel. In a vein they lie mainly in the tunica adventitia, and in large veins they can extend into the outer media, deeper than in arteries of the same size. In a section they show as small, thin-walled vessel profiles, some holding red cells, scattered through the outer wall.

The nervi vasorum ('nerves of the vessels') are the fine sympathetic nerve fibres that run in the tunica adventitia and supply the smooth muscle of the vein wall. The axons release noradrenaline, which makes the smooth muscle contract and narrow the vein, a process called venoconstriction. Venoconstriction moves blood out of the venous reservoir towards the heart, an important part of the early response to blood loss. They are hard to see in routine haematoxylin and eosin sections, so special nerve stains are needed.

Red blood cells (erythrocytes) are the most numerous cells in the blood flowing through the vein. They are biconcave, anucleate (nucleus-free) discs about 7.5 µm across and 2 µm thick at the rim, a shape that gives a large surface for gas exchange and lets them fold through the narrowest capillaries, which are only about 3 µm across. In a section they appear as pink, round profiles without a nucleus, which makes them easy to tell apart from the nucleated white cells.

A rolling leukocyte is a white blood cell, usually a neutrophil, that has been slowed by contact with the endothelial lining of a vein. Selectins, sticky adhesion molecules on the endothelium, make the cell tether and roll along the surface; integrins on the leukocyte then make it stop and squeeze between endothelial cells into the tissue, a process called diapedesis. This happens mainly in postcapillary venules, where most leukocytes leave the blood during acute inflammation.
